source: Schmidt & Rikers (2007) How expertise develops in medicine: knowledge encapsulation and illness script formation
finding: The intermediate effect (mid-level people recall more case detail than experts) is robust. Instructions to diagnose or to recall, and full or summary lab data, did not change it. Telling experts that national experts would grade their recall did not change it either.
numbers: Van de Wiel series: instructions and case form had no effect on effect size. De Bruin et al.: half the experts told they were being judged, no change in recall amount or kind. Eva et al.: effect also found in recognition, so it is not only a free-recall artefact.
limits: Review, not a new analysis. Authors are the theory holders. No pooled effect size is given.
agent_relevance: A good reasoner stores less case detail but the right detail. Do not score our agent by how much case text it echoes back; score the key features it keeps.

source: Schmidt & Rikers (2007) How expertise develops in medicine: knowledge encapsulation and illness script formation
finding: Two studies found expert recall beat intermediates, but only when experts were forced to comment on each finding. Without forced elaboration the intermediate effect returned. So the pattern is a default style of processing, not a ceiling on what experts can do.
numbers: Norman et al.: nephrologists vs advanced students on lab-only cases, experts recalled much more when they commented on each result. Verkoeijen et al.: same cases with and without clinical context, both gave an intermediate effect. Wimmers et al.: replicated Norman only with elaboration; control group without elaboration showed the intermediate effect again. A second expert-advantage study is called unexplained.
limits: Small number of studies, all from one research network. Lab-only cases are an unusual task.
agent_relevance: Forced item-by-item elaboration is a switch from compressed script use to detailed analysis. An S2 step that lists every finding will read like a novice; use it only when a script match is weak.

source: Schmidt & Rikers (2007) How expertise develops in medicine: knowledge encapsulation and illness script formation
finding: Causal (biomedical) knowledge helps diagnosis mostly after a delay, and learners spontaneously form short labels (encapsulations) for causal chains. Diagnostic accuracy at first test was equal for causal and feature-list learners; the causal group held up better one week later.
numbers: Woods et al. as summarised: both groups similar immediately; causal condition better after 1 week; recognition test with new encapsulating concepts favoured the causal group. Experts' protocols hold fewer biomedical and more encapsulating concepts than students'.
limits: Learners were students on artificial or simple disease sets in the cited work. Generalisation to real clinics is argued, not shown, in this review.
agent_relevance: A class library entry should carry a one-line causal reason for each key feature, not only a feature list. This is cheap to add and helps against drift.

source: Schmidt & Rikers (2007) How expertise develops in medicine: knowledge encapsulation and illness script formation
finding: Illness scripts are built from enabling conditions (who, when, where, risk context) more than from pathophysiology. The number of enabling conditions people name rises with expertise and with number of patients seen. One study also found effects of consequences, which the theory does not predict.
numbers: Custers 1998: enabling conditions mentioned rose with expertise level and with patients seen with that disease. Custers 1996: experts were sensitive to typicality of both enabling conditions and consequences; advanced students only to consequences. Van Schaik 2005 (GP referral): experienced doctors used enabling-condition information more, but consequences also moderated, against script theory. Hobus figure: experienced doctors generated more accurate hypotheses when cases carried enabling conditions.
limits: Measures are self-reported disease descriptions and small case sets. Hobus data are shown as a figure, not a tabled effect size.
agent_relevance: Put context fields (setting, prevalence, exposure, timeline) in S2 represent and in each class entry. They prune whole classes early, which fits base-rate guardrails.

source: Schmidt & Rikers (2007) How expertise develops in medicine: knowledge encapsulation and illness script formation
finding: Competing view: biomedical knowledge does not decay and is reached when a case is hard. Doctors explained 20 clinical constructs better than clerks and students, and experts used more biomedical concepts on difficult cases.
numbers: Van de Wiel 1999: doctors, clerks and advanced students explained 20 constructs; doctors gave more elaborate, more fluent and better explanations. Patel 1990: more biomedical concepts in expert protocols on difficult cases. Lexical decision studies (Rikers 2005) show fast access to biomedical terms.
limits: The authors say experimental work on this is still needed. It is an open debate in the review itself.
agent_relevance: Keep a deep-reasoning fallback. When a script fails, the agent should drop into mechanism-based reasoning rather than keep forcing a label.

source: Norman, Young & Brooks (2007) Non-analytical models of clinical reasoning: the role of experience
finding: Rival to script and encapsulation accounts: diagnosis rests partly on similarity to a specific stored case (exemplar), at all levels from novice to subspecialist. This is seen in dermatology, ECG and psychiatry. Early hypotheses from this fast route can change how later findings are read.
numbers: Abstract only read. Reviews mainly McMaster studies; no numbers recorded this session.
limits: Abstract only. Mostly the authors' own lab. Exemplar and script accounts are hard to tell apart with most designs.
agent_relevance: Class library should hold concrete past cases as well as abstract class summaries. Retrieval by similarity can anchor, so add a de-biasing pass.

source: Woods, Brooks & Norman (2007) It all make sense: biomedical knowledge, causal connections and memory in the novice diagnostician
finding: Learners given causal explanations for each feature of artificial diseases kept their diagnostic accuracy a week later; learners given features alone lost more. Experiment 2 showed learners lean more on causal information after a delay.
numbers: Exp 1: 89% correct (causal) vs 78% (no causal) at 1 week. Exp 2: mean probability of using causal information 57% vs 43% after delay. Sample sizes not recorded (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Artificial diseases, student volunteers.
agent_relevance: Supports pairing each class with a short why-note. The benefit shows later, not at first test, so judge it on delayed or repeated use.

source: Woods, Howey, Brooks & Norman (2006) Speed kills? Speed, accuracy, encapsulations and causal understanding
finding: Causal learners recognised encapsulating words better and did better when told to be fast, but worse when told to be thorough. This is a speed-accuracy crossover.
numbers: Study 1 (pseudo-endocrine diseases, psychology undergraduates): old words 90% vs 91%; encapsulated and novel consistent words 50% vs 41%, P=0.02. Study 2: speeded 71% vs 66% for causal group; thorough 67% vs 73%.
limits: Abstract only. Four artificial diseases, undergraduates, small effect of a few points. Possible ceiling and training-time effects.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: a causal, compressed model helps under fast mode and may hurt under slow mode. Match the mode to the stakes.

source: Kulasegaram et al. (2015) Cause and Effect: Testing a Mechanism and Method for the Cognitive Integration of Basic Science
finding: Putting basic science next to clinical content did not help; only explicit causal links did. Immediate diagnostic scores were equal in all four groups, and the causal group decayed least after a week.
numbers: N=94 first-year health professions students, 4 arms (causal, science-then-clinical, clinical-then-science, feature list). Condition x time interaction F(3,88)=3.05, P<.03, partial eta 0.10. No difference on memory quiz.
limits: Abstract only. Four disorders, short delay, student sample. Medium effect.
agent_relevance: Mere co-location of facts in a prompt is not integration. State the link between feature and mechanism explicitly.

source: Ark, Brooks & Eva (2006) Giving learners the best of both worlds: do clinical teachers need to guard against teaching pattern recognition to novices?
finding: Rival-theory test: feature-first and similarity-first instructions gave the same accuracy, but telling learners to use both together did better. This favours an additive model, not a choice between analytic and pattern routes.
numbers: N=48 psychology students, 4 groups of 12, 10 cardiac disorders on ECG. Feature first 42%, similarity 41% (p>.4), explicit combined 56%, implicit combined 53% (p<.01).
limits: Abstract only. Novices, not clinicians, tiny cells of 12. One domain (ECG).
agent_relevance: Run both routes: a fast match to a stored class and a feature check. Combine them instead of picking one.

source: Hatala, Brooks & Norman (2003) Practice makes perfect: the critical role of mixed practice in the acquisition of ECG interpretation skills
finding: Mixing examples from different categories during practice beat practising one category at a time. How the instruction was organised (features vs categories) made no difference.
numbers: Experiment 2: contrastive 46% vs non-contrastive 30% accuracy on novel ECGs, p<0.05. Experiment 1 no significant difference by instruction format. Group sizes not recorded.
limits: Abstract only. Medical students on ECG, one session.
agent_relevance: A class library works better when its entries are written to contrast with neighbours (what separates class A from B), not as isolated descriptions.

source: Coderre, Mandin, Harasym & Fick (2003) Diagnostic reasoning strategies and diagnostic success
finding: Think-aloud study in gastroenterology: odds of a correct diagnosis were higher with pattern recognition or scheme-inductive reasoning than with hypothetico-deduction. Expertise and the clinical presentation were independent predictors.
numbers: Logistic regression of strategy on success; exact odds ratios and sample size not read (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Observational: people use pattern recognition when it is easy, so the link may reflect case difficulty rather than strategy.
agent_relevance: Do not treat explicit hypothesis testing as the safe default. Prefer a quick scheme-based route and keep the slow route for mismatches.

source: Lambe, O'Reilly, Kelly & Curristan (2016) Dual-process cognitive interventions to enhance diagnostic reasoning: a systematic review
finding: Systematic review (not pooled) of interventions to help analytic and non-analytic reasoning. Many showed some effect. Guided reflection was the most consistently successful, and cognitive forcing helped accuracy and confidence. Measures were very mixed and mostly in early-career doctors.
numbers: 28 studies in five categories (educational, checklists, cognitive forcing, guided reflection, test instructions and others); guided reflection successful across 5 studies. No pooled effect size.
limits: Abstract only. Heterogeneous outcomes, mostly trainees, no meta-analytic estimate.
agent_relevance: Best-supported add-on to fast recognition is structured reflection (compare alternatives against the findings), not generic 'think carefully'.

source: Lubarsky, Charlin, Cook, Chalk & van der Vleuten (2011) Script concordance testing: a review of published validity evidence
finding: The Script Concordance Test (SCT) has good internal consistency and clear content rules. Scores correlate poorly with pure factual knowledge, more so in advanced learners. Evidence on response process and educational consequences is weak.
numbers: Validity framework with five categories; no pooled correlation reported in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Validity is context-bound. Few studies on how SCT affects learning.
agent_relevance: The SCT is a usable way to test whether an LLM updates a hypothesis the way experts do, which is script use rather than fact recall.

source: Dory, Gagnon, Vanpee & Charlin (2012) How to construct and implement script concordance tests: insights from a systematic review
finding: Practical design limits for SCTs: about 100 items from 25 to 30 cases is reliable, expert panels of 10 to 20 are needed, and the traditional aggregate scoring is satisfactory. Pass-mark setting for high stakes is unsettled.
numbers: 848 references found, 80 analysed. About 100 items (25% dropped after item analysis); panel 10-20.
limits: Abstract only. Evidence suits formative or medium stakes use.
agent_relevance: If we benchmark our agent on SCT items, we need about 100 items and a panel of 10+ experts; small item sets will be noisy.

source: Custers (2015) Thirty years of illness scripts: Theoretical origins and practical applications
finding: History review: the script idea came from general psychology, entered medicine through AI diagnostic systems, and was then specified by educators; it yielded the SCT. The author judges its base to be solid.
numbers: Narrative review; no figures read.
limits: Abstract only. Single author, favourable view of the concept.
agent_relevance: The illness script has an AI origin, so it maps naturally to a structured class library for an agent.

source: Moghadami, Amini, Moghadami, Dalal & Charlin (2021) Teaching clinical reasoning to undergraduate medical students by illness script method: a randomized controlled trial
finding: Teaching three diseases with an illness-script format beat teaching the signs-and-symptoms list on a knowledge test and on an SCT four weeks later. Both groups improved a lot, so the lecture route also worked.
numbers: N=100 fourth-year students, 50 per arm. Posttest 15.74 (SD 2.47) vs 14.38 (SD 2.59) out of 20, P=0.009, d=0.54. SCT 6.12 (SD 1.95) vs 4.54 (SD 1.56) out of 10, P=0.0001. Pre to post d about 2.0 in both groups. Pretest 10.87 vs 9.84, P=0.083.
limits: One school, three diseases, 7-hour workshop, same tutors for both arms, SCT is tied to taught cases; the intervention group still scored about 60% on SCT.
agent_relevance: A script-shaped format has a real but moderate edge over plain symptom lists. Expect the gain from structure to be modest compared with the gain from simply teaching the content.

source: Valente et al. (2026) 'Tell me what you know': Written recall as a window into illness script quality
finding: Free-recall text scored for accuracy, scope, organisation and encapsulation tracks training year. Most growth is by year 3, with little change after. Encapsulation terms were rare at every level, so the method did not pick up encapsulation.
numbers: Students from years 1 to 6 at seven Brazilian schools. Correct ideas for COPD median 3 (year 1) vs 14 (year 5); MI 8 vs 18 (p<0.01). Organisation 0.31 to 0.61 (COPD), 0.28 to 0.60 (MI). Progress-test correlation with correct ideas rho 0.56 (COPD), 0.46 (MI).
limits: Abstract only. Exploratory, cross-sectional, ceiling effect from time limit, only two diseases.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap test for an LLM class library: ask it to write what it knows about a disease, then score accuracy, scope, organisation (clustering).

source: Yanagita et al. (2024) Expert assessment of ChatGPT's ability to generate illness scripts
finding: GPT-4 produced illness scripts for 184 diseases with every requested field. Three physicians rated 56.0% as sufficient for students, 28.3% as partly lacking, and 15.8% as deficient. Cardiovascular and psychiatric scripts were weakest.
numbers: 184 diseases, GPT-4 version of 20 July 2023, items under 50 characters, three worked examples in the prompt. A 103, B 52, C 29. Cardiovascular: 6 of 14 rated C; psychiatric: 5 of 11 rated C; dermatology 0 of 13 C. Errors included wrong transmission route for varicella, vague diagnostics ('refer to guidelines') and outdated treatment (paper bag for hyperventilation).
limits: Three raters, no agreement figures, no standard for a good script, 3-point scale made by the authors, one model version, character limits may have caused omissions. The three example diseases were excluded from scoring.
agent_relevance: An LLM can draft the class library, but about 16% of entries would be flawed and it fails most on guideline-driven or criteria-driven diseases. Needs a check step before it is used as memory.

source: Savage, Nayak, Gallo, Rangan & Chen (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for large language model interpretability in medicine
finding: Prompting an LLM to follow human reasoning styles (differential, intuitive, analytic, Bayesian) did not beat plain chain-of-thought for GPT-4, and made GPT-3.5 worse. Telling a model HOW to reason did little for accuracy.
numbers: MedQA free-response, 518 test questions (95 for prompt tuning). GPT-3.5: CoT 46%, intuitive 48%, analytic 40% (-6.0, p=0.001), differential 38% (-8.9, p<0.001), Bayesian 42% (-4.4, p=0.02); zero-shot no CoT 31%. GPT-4 (498 usable): CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, differential 78%, analytic 78%, Bayesian 72% (-3.4, p=0.07). NEJM 310 cases (300 used): CoT 38% vs differential 34% (p=0.09).
quote: Prompts that focused on a single diagnostic reasoning strategy provided better results than prompts that combined multiple strategies.
limits: Two worked examples per prompt, one run each, MedQA is exam-style not real chart data, grading by the authors, single model family, GPT-4 version of 2023.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a reasoning-style prompt to raise accuracy by itself. The gain, if any, must come from the knowledge organisation (class library), checks and tests, not from style labels. Free-form step-by-step beat prescribed single strategies on the weaker model.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for large language model interpretability in medicine (rationale audit)
finding: When GPT-4 wrote differential-diagnosis rationales, wrong answers came with more logic errors than right answers. A reader could use the rationale as a signal of reliability, but not a perfect one.
numbers: 100 GPT-4 rationales: 65% of incorrect answers had false-logic statements (0.82 per rationale) vs 18% of correct answers (0.11 per rationale). Reviewers were blind to the question and the gold answer.
limits: Only 100 rationales, two reviewers, no confidence intervals in the text read, the first 100 items rather than a random sample.
agent_relevance: A rationale audit step (check each stated finding-to-class link) can flag likely wrong labels. It catches many, not all, errors.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial
finding: Giving doctors GPT-4 did not improve their diagnostic reasoning score, but GPT-4 alone scored higher than doctors with conventional resources. The tool was strong; the human use of it was the bottleneck.
numbers: N=50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), 6 vignettes, 60 minutes. Median score 76% (IQR 66-87) with LLM vs 74% (IQR 63-84) without; adjusted difference 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8; P=.60). Time per case 519 s vs 565 s (P=.20). LLM alone +16 points (95% CI 2-30; P=.03) over conventional group.
limits: Small sample, only 6 landmark cases, short session, little prompt training for users, LLM alone was run three times with a zero-shot prompt.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that returns a clear, ranked, checkable class list may matter more than raw model power; human-in-the-loop value is not automatic.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models
finding: LLMs lose accuracy when a case includes a bias cue. The cue that hurt most was false consensus; the cue that hurt least was confirmation. GPT-4 was the most robust model.
numbers: BiasMedQA, 1273 USMLE questions, 7 biases, 6 models. Unbiased accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, mixtral-8x7b 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama-13B 33.4%. Average drop with bias: GPT-4 -5.1%, mixtral -7.7%, GPT-3.5 -17.8%, Llama-2-70B -20.1%, PMC-Llama-13B -9.6%. By bias averaged across models: false consensus -24.9%, frequency -18.2%, recency -12.9%, confirmation -8.1%. GPT-4 false consensus -14.0%; confirmation -0.2%.
limits: Bias is injected as one short sentence, so it is a simple stand-in for real clinical bias. Multiple-choice format. Bias definitions follow human experiments but are not matched in strength.
agent_relevance: Our schema needs a guard against social-proof cues in the input (e.g. 'most doctors think it is X'); treat these as untrusted evidence for any class match.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models (mitigation)
finding: Simple prompt-level mitigation gave only partial recovery. Bias education, one-shot and few-shot demonstration each helped a little, and none restored unbiased accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4 reached 75.2% average under the few-shot mitigation. Mixtral best under education at 48.4%. GPT-3.5 gains: education +6.1% (p<1e-16), one-shot +4.3%, few-shot +5.2%.
limits: The authors state accuracy with mitigation still falls short of the no-bias level. Gains are in points of accuracy, from a lower base.
agent_relevance: A warning line in the prompt is not enough. Add a procedural check that re-scores the leading class with the bias-bearing sentence removed.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: o1-preview beat GPT-4 and physician baselines on differential diagnosis, reasoning documentation and management, using NEJM cases and a set of real emergency cases. The gain is on a recognition-and-differential task LLMs are good at.
numbers: NEJM CPC 143 cases: correct diagnosis in differential 78.3% (95% CI 70.7-84.8), first suggestion correct 52% (44-61). On 70 shared cases exact or very close 88.6% vs GPT-4 72.9% (p=.015). NEJM Healer 20 cases (80 responses): perfect R-IDEA 78/80 vs GPT-4 47/80, attendings 28/80, residents 16/80. Grey Matters management median 86% vs GPT-4 42%, physicians+GPT-4 41%, physicians 34%. ER 79 cases, exact or very close at triage 65.8% (o1) vs 54.4% and 48.1% for two attendings.
limits: Model-only, no human use; cases partly public so memorisation is possible (sensitivity analysis by date was done); ER task is a second opinion at preset touchpoints; text only; preprint at the time read.
agent_relevance: Strong recognition of the right class is available from the base model on case text. Our scaffold should aim at the failure cases, not at lifting the average of easy ones.

source: McDuff et al. (2023) Towards Accurate Differential Diagnosis with Large Language Models
finding: A fine-tuned PaLM 2 model beat unassisted doctors on difficult NEJM cases, and doctors with the model beat doctors with search. Fine-tuning for diagnosis gave a measurable gain.
numbers: 302 NEJM CPC cases, 20 clinicians, 2 clinicians per case. Model top-10 accuracy 59.1% (177 cases), top-1 29% (89 cases) vs unassisted clinicians top-10 33.6% (p=0.04). Clinicians top-10: unaided 36.1%, with search 44.4%, with LLM 51.7% (McNemar 45.7, p<0.01; vs search 4.75, p=0.03). Cases gained after assistance: 73 (LLM) vs 37 (search). Appropriateness: LLM 4.34 vs unassisted 3.74.
limits: Text-only cases (images and tables not fed to the model), automated grader used for part of the scoring, clinicians had no model-use training, cases are unusually hard and not typical practice, 2023 model.
agent_relevance: A recall-oriented, long differential list helps clinicians more than a short one. The list also got longer (median 8 vs 6), so check that breadth was not the only gain.

source: Safranek et al. (2026) Simulated evaluation of large language model stepwise diagnostic reasoning with real-world chest pain encounters and Bayesian networks
finding: Without prevalence cues, GPT-4o over-predicted rare, life-threatening diagnoses: high sensitivity, poor specificity. Adding base-rate cues or removing the forced menu raised specificity a lot but wrecked sensitivity. A good trade-off was not found by prompt changes.
numbers: 500 ED chest-pain cases drawn from 202,632; life-threatening causes 2.14% (ACS 1.04% to oesophageal rupture 0.01%). Baseline sensitivity 79.3%, specificity 45.2%. Prevalence cues: specificity 83.0%, sensitivity 30.4%, 107 fewer false alarms per 500. No category constraint: specificity 94.7%, sensitivity 8.8%, 140 fewer false alarms per 500. Rank overlap with the Bayesian optimal question order 0.060-0.097; more imaging requests (30%+) than clinicians.
limits: One model (GPT-4o), one complaint (chest pain), seven target diagnoses plus Other; missing data filled by a Bayesian network model, so the simulation is partly synthetic.
agent_relevance: Direct hit on a script weakness: LLMs lack calibrated prevalence in their classes. The class library should store base rates and the schema should keep them separate from feature fit.

source: Hudon et al. (2024) Using ChatGPT in Psychiatry to Design Script Concordance Tests in Undergraduate Medical Education
finding: Psychiatrists and residents could not reliably tell ChatGPT-written SCTs from expert-written ones; ratings of scenarios and questions were similar. The ChatGPT items were too caricatured and simple.
numbers: 102 respondents (45 residents, 57 teaching psychiatrists), 6 SCTs, 3 by experts and 3 by ChatGPT. Scenario rating 66.4% (expert) vs 67.2% (ChatGPT), P=.84; clinical questions 70.05% vs 68.8%, P=.99; expert opinion item P=.07. Detected as AI-generated: 54% vs 40%.
limits: Response rate 16.1% (102 of 635). Three items per arm, psychiatry only. Comments from 39 respondents.
agent_relevance: LLMs write typical, textbook-like cases well and miss the messy ones. This matches the typicality bias expected of a class library built from text.

source: Sallam & Abouzeid (2025) Introducing AI as members of script concordance test expert reference panel
finding: ChatGPT-4 and o1 acted as panel members for an ophthalmology SCT. Human experts scored highest on most vignettes; o1 was closer to the experts than GPT-4. Models cannot replace the experts but can fill out a panel.
numbers: Traditional panel of 15 (5 residents, 5 lecturers, 5 professors) vs AI panel; per-vignette means only, no single effect size read.
limits: Abstract only. One specialty, one clerkship, quasi-experimental.
agent_relevance: Models can imitate a mid-level panel but compress variation between experience levels.

source: Lilamand et al. (2026) Evaluating how different versions of ChatGPT align with expert opinions on geriatric script concordance tests
finding: On 20 geriatric SCT items ChatGPT-4 and ChatGPT-5 scored about as well as experts; GPT-3.5 was far lower; GPT-4o was in between. SCT scores track model generation.
numbers: 20 validated items, 43 experts. GPT-3.5 8/20 (agreed with the expert majority on 15% of responses); GPT-4 15.6/20 and GPT-5 15.2/20 (majority agreement 45%); GPT-4o 13.6/20.
limits: Abstract only. 20 items is below the Dory 2012 guide of about 100, so scores are noisy. One specialty.
agent_relevance: SCT gives a script-level test for LLM updating of hypotheses. A 45% majority match leaves a lot of room for the schema to help.

source: Qazi et al. (2026) Automation Bias in Large Language Model-Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning among Physicians Trained in AI Literacy
finding: Doctors who had 20 hours of AI-literacy training still followed wrong LLM suggestions. Their accuracy dropped when suggestions carried planted errors.
numbers: 44 physicians (22 per arm), 264 cases, 3 of 6 vignettes with errors in treatment arm. Composite accuracy 73.3% vs 84.9% (adjusted -14.0 points, 95% CI -18.9 to -9.1). Top-choice 76.1% vs 90.5% (-18.3 points, 95% CI -26.6 to -10.0).
limits: Abstract only. Single country, small sample, fixed planted errors, vignettes not real patients.
agent_relevance: If a downstream human relies on our agent, a confident wrong class label does more harm than a hedged list. Show the evidence and the competing classes.

source: Coskun, Kiyak, Coskun, Budakoglu & Ozdemir (2025) Large language models for generating script concordance test in obstetrics and gynecology: ChatGPT and Claude
finding: ChatGPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet wrote SCT items that 16 panellists rated as meeting quality criteria about nine times in ten. Weakest criterion was difficulty for students.
numbers: Overall agreement 90.57% (ChatGPT-4o) and 91.48% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet); difficulty criterion 71.25% and 76.25%. Five topics, 11 criteria.
limits: Abstract only. Five topics, no test of whether the items discriminate learners from experts.
agent_relevance: LLM-made class descriptions look acceptable on face review. Face validity does not show that they separate close mimics.
